To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

estrogen treatment induces uterine growth by inducing the expression of a set of genes that are involved in the regulation of the cell cycle, and that these genes are expressed in a temporally ordered fashion.

the estrogen-induced uterotropic response can be modeled using gene expression data, that the uterotrophic response can be divided into three phases based on the gene expression profile, that the uterotropic response is characterized by the expression of genes involved in cell growth and cell cycle control, that the expression of these genes is regulated by the estrogen receptor, that the utero-protective effect of antiestrogens is mediated by the estrogen receptor and that the expression profile is consistent with estrogen-induced utero

gene expression profiles can be used to predict uterotrophic responses in vivo, and that the uterotrophic response is associated with the up-regulation of genes involved in the regulation of cell cycle progression, cell division, and cell proliferation, as well as with the down-regulation of genes associated with the regulation of cell adhesion, cell differentiation, and cell death.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a systems biology approach to the study of the rodent uterine response to estrogens.
the use of gene expression analysis to understand the transcription of the uterotrophic response.
the use of gene expression profiles to understand the molecular basis of physiological and pathological processes, and the use of these profiles in predictive toxicology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the estrogen-induced uterotropic response is a highly complex phenomenon, which involves the coordinated action of many genes.

gene expression changes are associated with uterine growth, and these changes are consistent with the hypothesis that estrogen induces the uterine growth through an estrogen receptor-dependent mechanism.

gene expression profiling is a powerful tool for the identification of molecular mechanisms underlying the uterotrophic response, but that further research is required to establish a mechanistic link between the transcriptional changes and physiological and pathological events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the estrogenic induction of gene expression is associated with the induction of uterine growth, that the estrogenic regulation of gene expression is tissue-specific, and that estrogen-regulated genes are not necessarily associated with estrogen-induced physiological changes.
estrogen-induced uteronephritis is associated with a complex transcriptional response that is highly tissue- and time-dependent.

the transcriptional changes associated with estrogen-induced rodent uterine growth can be understood in terms of a small set of genes that are involved in the regulation of cell proliferation and cell differentiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gene expression profiling is an excellent tool for the identification of transcriptional events that are associated with estrogen-induced growth of the rat uterus.

a gene expression signature can be used to predict the magnitude of the uterine response and that the genes in this signature are enriched in the functional categories of cell cycle regulation and DNA replication, which are known to be important for the estrogen-induced uterotrophic response.
the transcriptional program induced by estrogens can be used to predict the magnitude of uterine growth and to identify genes that are likely to play a role in estrogen action.
